newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council will probably delay sanctions on UNITA.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council will probably delay sanctions on UNITA.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Friday said UNITA's compliance with the peace accords were unsatisfactory but diplomats said he wanted a delay in any sanctions imposed on the rebel movement.

They said the Security Council next week might impose sanctions but give a two-week grace period before they went into effect. Or it might postpone any resolution until September while the United Nations verifies new proposals from UNITA.

Annan also recommended the planned withdrawal of U.N. troops from Angola be put back at least six weeks. In light of the uneasy peace in Angola, he said up to 2,650 soldiers should stay until the end of October.

In a report to the Security Council, Annan said no signficant progress had been made and that UNITA's last-minute overtures to avert sanctions were not acceptable, a trigger for the council to consider sanctions.
The council had threatened sanctions against UNITA if it did not comply with its demands by the time Annan issued his report and diplomats said these would be discussed next week.

But the envoys said since the report, written on Thursday, U.N. officials in Luanada wanted to verify UNITA's latest proposed concessions in extending government control over its territory, changing the nature of its radio station and giving more accurate figures on how many men it still had under arms.
The Angola government itself, they said, would rather call UNITA's bluff than have sanctions imposed immediately, which they believed were hard to enforce.

Possible sanctions could include a travel ban against UNITA leader Dr. Jonas Savimbi and other officials. Other measures, such as freezing UNITA bank accounts abroad, are being considered but might not be enacted until a later date because of the difficulty in carring them out.

The council had previously imposed an arms embargo but apparently UNITA is able to keep open its supply lines despite the fall of President Mobutu Sese Seko in the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo, formerly Zaire. Mobutu was one of UNITA's principal backers.
Annan, in the report, said he was confident the Security Council would "continue to exercise its authority and take all necessary steps to ensure full compliance with its decisions."

The council has demanded of UNITA that it demilitarize all its forces, transform its radio station into a non-partisan broadcasting facility and cooperate fully in extending government administration throughout the country as required in 1994 peace agreements signed in Lusaka, Zambia.

After two decades of civil war, UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, entered into a unity government in April with the MPLA, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola.
The conflict became a superpower proxy fight with the United States and the former white government of South Africa supporting Savimbi and the Soviet Union and Cuba supporting the now-ruling MPLA.

But UNITA still controls about 70 percent of the country, including Angola's diamond mines, and only a minority of its fighters have been demobilized and incorporated into a new national Angolan army.

Fears are growing that the peace process has been unraveling since the recent civil war in the neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo, whose former ruler Mobutu Sese Seke had aided UNITA's campaign.

In May and in June the government launched an offensive into UNITA zones in the northeast, in what military officials in Luanda said was the biggest such operation since 1994 and a sign that positions were hardening.
They did this after large numbers of UNITA soldiers returned to Angola after fighting alongside of Mobutu's forces against rebels loyal to now-President Laurent Kabila.
